label: Roots: disassemblers, source drops and the law (1990-1999)
blurb: Commercial disassemblers appear, courts and lawmakers carve out room for reverse engineering, and id Software starts the habit of opening old engines.

events.title: IDA, the Interactive Disassembler, is released
events.body: Ilfak Guilfanov's interactive disassembler ships after a year of work. It becomes the standard commercial tool for reading machine code for the next three decades.

events.title: EU Software Directive allows decompilation for interoperability
events.body: The European Union's 1991 software directive explicitly permits decompiling a program when it is needed to make independent software work with it, giving European reverse engineers a statutory footing.

events.title: Sega v. Accolade: disassembly can be fair use
events.body: The US Ninth Circuit rules that disassembling a program to understand its functional interfaces can be fair use when there is no other way to get at those ideas. The decision underpins much later US reverse engineering.
events.who: US Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit

events.title: The Wine project starts
events.body: Bob Amstadt and Eric Youngdale begin Wine, a clean reimplementation of the Windows API so Windows programs can run on Unix-like systems.

events.title: Cristina Cifuentes' thesis on reverse compilation
events.body: Cifuentes' PhD thesis "Reverse Compilation Techniques" lays out the structure of a general-purpose decompiler, an academic reference point for later decompilers.

events.title: "Abandonware" gets its name
events.body: Peter Ringering coins the term for software no longer sold or supported; an Abandonware Ring of sites forms in early 1997 to share such games, drawing industry cease-and-desist letters later that year.

events.title: MAME 0.1 is released
events.body: The Multiple Arcade Machine Emulator project publishes its first version, starting a long effort to document and preserve arcade hardware in code. MAME later became free software in 2016.

events.title: id Software releases the Doom source code
events.body: John Carmack publishes the Doom source code (the copy id later put on GitHub is GPL 2.0), which spawns decades of source ports and shows a game can outlive its platform through its code.

events.title: ReactOS development begins
events.body: After the stalled FreeWin95 effort, developers restart as ReactOS: an open-source operating system aiming for binary compatibility with Windows NT, written without Microsoft code.

events.title: Home of the Underdogs opens
events.body: Sarinee Achavanuntakul launches an abandonware archive with reviews and downloads for thousands of out-of-print PC games, an early model for community game preservation.

events.title: DMCA signed into US law
events.body: The Digital Millennium Copyright Act adds anti-circumvention rules that shape how preservationists and reverse engineers can handle protected software, and later becomes the usual tool for takedowns of fan ports.

events.title: Quake engine source released under the GPL
events.body: id Software opens the Quake engine, continuing the practice of releasing engine code once a game's commercial life winds down.

label: Reimplementations and real decompilers (2000-2012)
blurb: Emulation gets legal cover, fans rebuild whole games from scratch, and decompilation becomes a commercial product.

events.title: Sony v. Connectix upholds reverse engineering for emulation
events.body: The Ninth Circuit finds that copying Sony's BIOS while reverse engineering it to build the Virtual Game Station emulator was fair use, building on Sega v. Accolade.
events.who: US Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit

events.title: ScummVM begins
events.body: Ludvig Strigeus starts a reimplementation of LucasArts' SCUMM adventure engine, later joined by Vincent Hamm; it grows into a host for many classic adventure engines.

events.title: OpenTTD 0.1
events.body: Ludvig Strigeus releases a re-engineered Transport Tycoon Deluxe, converted from the 1994 assembly original to C, which becomes a long-lived open-source game.

events.title: Quake III Arena source released
events.body: Following a QuakeCon 2005 announcement, id Tech 3 is released under the GPL.

events.title: Hex-Rays Decompiler launches
events.body: Hex-Rays introduces a commercial decompiler plugin for IDA that turns machine code into C-like pseudocode, making decompilation an everyday reverse engineering tool.

events.title: Wine 1.0
events.body: Fifteen years after it started, Wine reaches version 1.0.

events.title: pret's Pokémon disassemblies on GitHub
events.body: The pokecrystal disassembly repository goes up on GitHub, part of the pret group's work to rebuild Game Boy Pokémon games as assembly that reassembles into the original ROMs.

label: Archives in the browser (2013-2018)
blurb: Preservation moves online and fans start rebuilding classic PC games from their binaries.

events.title: Internet Archive opens the Console Living Room
events.body: The Internet Archive adds hundreds of early console games playable in the browser through the JSMESS emulator, as part of its historical software collection.

events.title: OpenRCT2 development starts
events.body: Ted "IntelOrca" John begins an open-source recreation of RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 in C++, which still needs the original game's data to run.

events.title: Ghidra's existence revealed
events.body: The WikiLeaks Vault 7 documents first reveal that the NSA has an internal reverse engineering framework called Ghidra.

events.title: Devilution reconstructs Diablo's source
events.body: Using symbol information left on the Japanese PlayStation release and a hidden debug build, contributors rebuild Diablo's source code; DevilutionX later carries it to modern systems.

label: The matching-decomp boom (2019-2023)
blurb: Free professional tooling arrives and N64 decompilations that rebuild byte-identical ROMs turn into native PC ports.

events.title: NSA releases Ghidra
events.body: Ghidra is released for free at the RSA Conference, with source on GitHub about a month later, giving everyone a capable decompiler without an IDA licence.

events.title: Super Mario 64 decompilation goes public
events.body: The n64decomp group publishes a C decompilation of Super Mario 64 that rebuilds matching ROMs, an early large N64 matching decomp and a template for many that follow.

events.title: Ars Technica explains the N64 decomp scene
events.body: A widely read feature describes how hobbyists turn N64 binaries back into compilable C, prompted by a playable PC port of Super Mario 64 built on the decomp.

events.title: Nintendo targets the Super Mario 64 PC port
events.body: Takedown notices go after sites hosting compiled builds of the fan PC port and videos of it; the source-only decomp itself stays up.

events.title: Internet Archive preserves Flash with Ruffle
events.body: Ahead of Flash Player's end of life at the close of 2020, the Internet Archive starts playing Flash animations and games in the browser through the Rust-based Ruffle emulator.

events.title: Take-Two DMCA takes down re3
events.body: Take-Two files a DMCA notice against re3, the reverse-engineered GTA III code, and GitHub disables the whole fork network; Take-Two follows with legal action in September 2021.

events.title: decomp.me appears
events.body: A collaborative website for matching decompilation goes up, letting people share single-function "scratches" and work on them together in the browser.

events.title: Ocarina of Time code fully decompiled
events.body: The Zelda Reverse Engineering Team reports that all of Ocarina of Time's game code has been turned into C, opening the way to ports and mods.

events.title: Asahi Linux alpha
events.body: The first public Asahi Linux alpha installs on M1-series Macs, aimed at developers and power users.

events.title: Ship of Harkinian released
events.body: Harbour Masters release an unofficial native PC port of Ocarina of Time built on the OoT decompilation; players supply their own ROM for the assets.

events.title: OpenGOAL's first release
events.body: The OpenGOAL project, which decompiles Jak and Daxter's GOAL code and rebuilds the game natively for PC, publishes its first tagged release.

events.title: Perfect Dark decompilation reported complete
events.body: Ryan Dwyer's Perfect Dark decompilation covers the NTSC versions of the game, a prerequisite for the later native port.

events.title: Study: 87% of classic games are out of print
events.body: A Video Game History Foundation and Software Preservation Network survey finds that 87% of classic US-released games are not commercially available.
events.who: Video Game History Foundation, Software Preservation Network

label: Recompilation goes mainstream (2024-2025)
blurb: Static recompilers make native ports possible without a finished decomp, and LLMs enter decompilation research.

events.title: LLM4Decompile paper
events.body: Researchers publish open language models trained to decompile binaries to C, one of the first widely cited LLM decompilers.
events.who: Hanzhuo Tan, Qi Luo, Jing Li, Yuqun Zhang

events.title: N64: Recompiled and Zelda 64: Recompiled
events.body: Mr-Wiseguy releases a static recompiler for N64 code together with a native PC port of Majora's Mask built with it; the player supplies the ROM.

events.title: 2 Ship 2 Harkinian 1.0
events.body: Harbour Masters' decomp-based Majora's Mask PC port ships its first release, weeks after the recompiled version.

events.title: decomp.dev progress site
events.body: A shared progress site and GitHub bot starts tracking how far participating decomp projects have matched.

events.title: Starship, a Star Fox 64 PC port
events.body: Harbour Masters release Starship, a native Star Fox 64 port built on the SF64 decompilation and libultraship.

events.title: EA releases classic Command & Conquer source
events.body: Electronic Arts publishes GPL source for Tiberian Dawn, Red Alert, Renegade and Generals/Zero Hour for preservation, without game assets.

events.title: Unleashed Recompiled and XenonRecomp
events.body: A static recompilation of the Xbox 360 Sonic Unleashed ships as a native PC port, using the XenonRecomp and XenosRecomp tools and inspired by N64: Recompiled.

label: Completion and the AI debate (2026)
blurb: Long-running decomps finish while AI-generated "recomps" flood in and the community starts labelling human-made work.

events.title: Banjo: Recompiled 1.0
events.body: A native PC port of Banjo-Kazooie built with N64: Recompiled on top of the Banjo-Kazooie decompilation reaches 1.0.

events.title: AI-assisted Mario Kart Wii recomp stirs debate
events.body: The announcement of a statically recompiled Mario Kart Wii port that openly uses AI coding agents splits the community over code quality and maintainability.

events.title: GoldenEye 007 reaches 100% decompiled
events.body: The GoldenEye decompilation reports 100% for the US, Japanese and PAL versions after years of work; builds still need a user-supplied ROM.

events.title: A list of human-made decomps and recomps
events.body: X user Funky90sLion starts a public document cataloguing decomp and recomp projects made without generative AI, covered by Retro Dodo the next day.

events.title: Banjo: Recompiled lead calls AI ports "a race to the bottom"
events.body: DarioSamo distances his team from an AI-generated Banjo-Tooie recomp and criticises reuse of his team's work in that way.

events.title: Recomp developers push back on "slopcomps"
events.body: Kotaku reports on the backlash against vibe-coded N64 ports, with the Zelda and Banjo recomp teams restating their no-AI policies.

events.title: Beetle Adventure Racing decomp team objects to AI recomp
events.body: Synamax says his volunteer team's in-progress Beetle Adventure Racing decomp was taken and "finished" with an LLM without consent, and commits to finishing a human-made version.
